surveyDefinition.title: Smartwatches — consumer survey (U.S.)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on smartwatch ownership, usage intensity, purchase drivers, and unmet needs.

segments.name: Health-Focused Buyers
segments.description: Own a smartwatch primarily for health and fitness tracking; use it daily for workouts, heart rate, sleep; willing to pay more for advanced sensors and accuracy; frustrated by battery life and data reliability.

segments.name: Ecosystem-Loyal Users
segments.description: Own a smartwatch that integrates tightly with their smartphone brand; value notifications, convenience, and seamless sync; less price-sensitive; unlikely to switch ecosystems.

segments.name: Style-Conscious Buyers
segments.description: Choose a smartwatch as a fashion accessory as much as a tech device; prioritize design, materials, and customization; moderate usage; may own multiple bands or watches.

segments.name: Budget-Conscious Pragmatists
segments.description: Want basic smartwatch features (notifications, step counting) at a low price; highly price-sensitive; often consider fitness bands as alternatives; frustrated by cost and value.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Smartwatches buyers in U.S.. It asks how people use Smartwatches, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in U.S. who buy or use Smartwatches for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who currently own or have purchased a smartwatch in the past 12 months; Individuals who are actively considering purchasing a smartwatch within the next 6 months; Adults aged 18+ who make their own purchase decisions. Excluded: Businesses or institutions purchasing smartwatches in bulk for employees; Children under 18 (unless the study specifically targets kids' smartwatches, which is not the primary market); Individuals who only use basic fitness bands without smart features.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model and brand themselves. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining purchase is by individual consumers, making this a pure B2C market.
respondentBehaviours: Health and fitness tracking (steps, heart rate, sleep)
Smartphone integration for notifications and calls
Brand loyalty to smartphone ecosystems (Apple, Samsung, etc.)
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how it fits into their daily life — how often they wear it, for what purposes, and who in the household uses it. It then moves to the purchase journey: what triggered the buy, where they researched and bought, how much they spent, and what features decided the choice. Next, it digs into what they need from the device — must-have features, battery and accuracy expectations, comfort and design, app experience, and trade-offs — ending with perceived value. Finally, it measures satisfaction, identifies pain points, and explores switching…

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Smartwatches in U.S. — who Individuals who currently own or have purchased a smartwatch in the past 12 months; Individuals who are actively considering purchasing a smartwatch within the next 6 months; Adults aged 18+ who make their own purchase decisions. The audience is defined as individual consumers who buy smartwatches for personal use, as they are the primary purchasers and decision-makers. The demographic and behavioral criteria capture both current owners and potential buyers to support a broad consumer survey.

exclusions: Businesses or institutions purchasing smartwatches in bulk for employees

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on smartwatch ownership, usage intensity, purchase drivers, and unmet needs.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Combination of usage/behavioural and jobs-to-be-done: the smartwatch category is split by how deeply the device is woven into daily life (fitness, health, notifications, style) and what job it is hired to do — fitness tracking, health monitoring, connectivity, or fashion. This lens separates buyers

segments.name: Health-Focused Buyers
segments.description: Own a smartwatch primarily for health and fitness tracking; use it daily for workouts, heart rate, sleep; willing to pay more for advanced sensors and accuracy; frustrated by battery life and data reliability.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report high usage frequency, prioritize health features over style, and express strong interest in advanced health monitoring (blood pressure, glucose).

segments.name: Ecosystem-Loyal Users
segments.description: Own a smartwatch that integrates tightly with their smartphone brand; value notifications, convenience, and seamless sync; less price-sensitive; unlikely to switch ecosystems.
segments.hypothesis: This group will show high brand loyalty, rate ecosystem integration as a top driver, and be less concerned about price than about compatibility.

segments.name: Style-Conscious Buyers
segments.description: Choose a smartwatch as a fashion accessory as much as a tech device; prioritize design, materials, and customization; moderate usage; may own multiple bands or watches.
segments.hypothesis: This group will rate design and style as top decision drivers, show moderate usage frequency, and be willing to pay a premium for aesthetics.

segments.name: Budget-Conscious Pragmatists
segments.description: Want basic smartwatch features (notifications, step counting) at a low price; highly price-sensitive; often consider fitness bands as alternatives; frustrated by cost and value.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report lower spend, prioritize price over advanced features, and show higher switching propensity for cheaper alternatives.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question 'cp7' (main reason wanted a smartwatch) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it explicitly asks for the primary motivation, cleanly separating health tracking, notification convenience, and style.
notes: Scoring focuses on direct motivational and behavioural indicators; many generic satisfaction and demographic questions left unscored.
Budget pragmatists are identified by low spend, price sensitivity, and willingness to give up features.
Ecosystem loyalists are identified by same-brand ownership, notification focus, and seamless sync importance.
Health optimizers are identified by health/fitness motivation, frequent wear, and health data concerns.
Style conscious are identified by fashion/luxury choices, design priorities, and premium expectations.
4 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how it fits into their daily life — how often they wear it, for what purposes, and who in the household uses it. It then moves to the purchase journey: what triggered the buy, where they researched and bought, how much they spent, and what features decided the choice. Next, it digs into what they need from the device — must-have features, battery and accuracy expectations, comfort and design, app experience, and trade-offs — ending with perceived value. Finally, it measures satisfaction, identifies pain points, and explores switching…
storyline_notes: Replaced generic 'category relationship' with 'smartwatch ownership' to immediately screen for owners and non-owners.
Added 'battery and accuracy' as a distinct beat in preferences because battery life and sensor accuracy are the top pain points in the market profile.
Added 'app and ecosystem' beat to capture the importance of smartphone integration, a key purchase driver and pain point.
In buying behavior, included 'price paid' as a spend beat, and placed 'decision drivers' last to capture the final choice criteria.
In satisfaction, added 'pain points' as a friction beat, and 'upgrade intent' as the final future-use beat, reflecting the high-growth upgrade market.
All beats are answerable with closed questions and avoid asking age, income, or geography directly.
metadata.classification_reason: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model and brand themselves. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining purchase is by individual consumers, making this a pure B2C market.
